sections.title: Situation
sections.prompt: What is the council really deciding, and which numbers frame it?
criteria: Identifies in-house data engineering on customer data (84 requested, 60 available) as the binding constraint
Shows that ML capacity and budget are not the binding constraints
Notes that the $39M of claims rests on different kinds of evidence and can't be added as is
Spots that P1, P2 and P8 draw on the same care calls

sections.title: Stakeholders
sections.prompt: Who has a stake, what does each want, and how do you bring them along?
criteria: Covers the CFO and at least four of the five sponsoring executives
Says what the unfunded sponsors (P7, P8) get instead of a flat no
Includes the data engineers and their load
Ends with one idea that ties the stakeholders together

sections.title: Options
sections.prompt: What are the real ways to build the portfolio, and how does each compare?
criteria: Compares at least two ranking methods, including ranking by claimed benefit
Shows that moving non-customer-data work (P4, P5) to contractors frees the bottleneck
Shows what spreading the bottleneck across everyone does
Compares options on one table with funded set, months used and weighted value

sections.title: Decision and Trade-offs
sections.prompt: Which proposals are in, which are out, and what would change the line?
criteria: Draws one clear cut line with every proposal placed
Funds P1 in stages with a measurable gate
Names a fallback for the freed capacity if P1's gate fails
Justifies P6 as a risk decision rather than on ROI alone

sections.title: Economics
sections.prompt: What is each proposal worth after weights and overlaps, and what does the portfolio cost?
criteria: Applies finance's weights to every claim and uses P3's measured effect (0.03, not 0.05)
Removes the P1 and P2 overlap with a stated calculation
Ranks by weighted benefit per in-house data-engineer-month
Separates new spend ($4.2M) from payroll ($2.71M) and gives the portfolio total

sections.title: Org and Ownership
sections.prompt: Who decides, who owns each benefit, and who measures it?
criteria: Names a single accountable owner for the portfolio
Makes each sponsor own their benefit figure as weighted
Has finance, not sponsors, measure realized benefit
Makes re-allocating data-engineer months a council decision

sections.title: Plan and Milestones
sections.prompt: What happens through the year, and where can money and people move?
criteria: Includes a dated P1 gate with a measurable threshold
Has a quarterly review with a rule for stopping under-delivering projects
Puts P6 through a shadow phase before it blocks customers
Ends with next year's portfolio informed by measured results

sections.title: Risk and Governance
sections.prompt: What could go wrong with the portfolio, and what controls it?
criteria: Quantifies how fragile the bottleneck is (93% allocated; one leaver costs about 12 months)
Keeps contractors off customer data with access controls
Guards P1 against deflection that comes back as repeat calls
Addresses benefits failing to materialize with a concrete rule

sections.title: Metrics
sections.prompt: How will the council know a year from now whether the portfolio worked?
criteria: Pairs each success metric with a guard metric
Measures realized against weighted benefit per project
Reports project by project, not only the portfolio total

sections.title: Communication
sections.prompt: What does each executive hear, and how often?
criteria: Gives a one-line message for at least four audiences
Tells the CFO weighted benefit, new spend and payroll separately
Pre-wires the unfunded sponsors before the council meets
Sets a cadence and says failed gates and missed benefits are reported
